blocks.text: The chapter presents high priesthood as an honor conferred by God, not a position someone claims independently. It first applies that principle to Aaron and then to Christ: Jesus does not appoint or glorify himself as high priest but is acclaimed by God as a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

The declarations quoted in verses 5-6 reflect a broader New Testament practice of quoting and echoing psalms when discussing Jesus. Such appeals appear in arguments about subjects including his suffering, resurrection, enthronement, priesthood, mission, and worship. Here, the quotations belong specifically to the chapter’s presentation of Jesus as Son and priest, although the precise contours of this wider pattern remain a matter of interpretation.

Papyrus 46 is an early substantial manuscript witness to Hebrews, though portions are missing and its date, estimated from handwriting, remains approximate. Codex Sinaiticus also preserves Hebrews, placing it in its New Testament sequence after 2 Thessalonians. These details concern the transmission and arrangement of Hebrews as a whole rather than serving as direct anchors for this chapter.
